young.html: In ancient Athens, plays were part of a great spring festival for the god Dionysus. Thousands of people sat on a hillside to watch, and poets competed for a prize. Aeschylus was the first great writer of tragedies, serious plays about gods, kings and hard choices.

His most famous work is three plays told together, the Oresteia. It is the story of a royal family with a curse on it. When King Agamemnon comes home from the Trojan War, his wife Clytemnestra kills him, because years before he sacrificed their daughter to get winds for his ships. Their son Orestes grows up and takes revenge on his mother. Then the Furies, spirits of revenge, hunt Orestes. It looks as if the killing will never stop.

Then something new happens. The goddess Athena says: let's have a trial. She picks citizens of Athens to be a jury, hears both sides, and the vote decides. Even the angry Furies are persuaded to accept it, and they become protectors of the city. Revenge gives way to a court of law.

young.cap: The family of Atreus. Tap a name to learn who they are; choose a play to see who is in it.

young.html: Hold a trial. Pick a small family argument (who gets the last cookie, whose turn it is to choose the movie). One person speaks for each side, and everyone else is the jury and votes. Afterward, talk about it: was a vote fairer than letting the loudest person win? What made a good argument?

full.html: Aeschylus (c. 525–456 BC) was born at Eleusis, near Athens. He fought against the Persians at Marathon in 490 BC, where his brother was killed, and probably at Salamis in 480 BC. He wrote perhaps 70 to 90 plays and won first prize at the festival of Dionysus about 13 times. Only seven of his plays survive, and one of those, Prometheus Bound, may not be his. Aristotle says he added a second actor, which made real dialogue possible. He died at Gela in Sicily; his epitaph, as reported later, recalls his courage at Marathon and says nothing of his plays.

The Oresteia (458 BC) is the only complete trilogy of Greek tragedy that survives: Agamemnon, The Libation Bearers (Choephori) and The Eumenides. It won first prize. A fourth, comic "satyr play" performed with it is lost.
A watchman on the palace roof at Argos waits, night after night, for a chain of beacon fires to signal that Troy has fallen:

full.text: So now I am still watching for the signal-flame, the gleaming fire that is to bring news from Troy and tidings of its capture.
full.author: Aeschylus
full.ed: Loeb Classical Library, Heinemann and G. P. Putnam's Sons

full.html: The chorus of old men remembers how Agamemnon, ten years before, sacrificed his daughter Iphigenia when the goddess Artemis held back the winds his fleet needed. They search for meaning in suffering:

full.text: Zeus, who sets mortals on the path to understanding, Zeus, who has established as a fixed law that wisdom comes by suffering.
full.author: Aeschylus
full.ed: Loeb Classical Library, Heinemann and G. P. Putnam's Sons

full.html: Agamemnon returns with the Trojan princess Cassandra, a prophet no one believes. Clytemnestra welcomes him with a purple carpet and kills him offstage, with her ally Aegisthus, Agamemnon's cousin and an heir of the family feud. The audience hears it rather than sees it.

full.text: The Libation Bearers and The Eumenides

full.html: Years later Orestes returns in secret and meets his sister Electra at their father's tomb. Commanded by Apollo, he kills Aegisthus and his mother. At once the Furies (Erinyes), ancient goddesses who punish crimes against kin, begin to hunt him.
In the third play Orestes flees to Apollo's shrine at Delphi and then to Athens. Athena does not judge the case herself. She founds a court on the Areopagus, the Hill of Ares, with citizen jurors:

full.text: Hear now my ordinance, people of Attica, as you judge the first trial for bloodshed. In the future, even as now, this court of judges will always exist for the people of Aegeus. … Neither anarchy nor tyranny—this I counsel my citizens to support and respect, and not to drive fear wholly out of the city.
full.author: Aeschylus
full.ed: Loeb Classical Library, Heinemann and G. P. Putnam's Sons
full.note: Shortened where marked. Aegeus was a legendary king of Athens.

full.html: The votes are equal; Athena's deciding vote frees Orestes. The Furies threaten the land, but Athena persuades them with offers of honor, and they accept a home in Athens as the Eumenides, "the Kindly Ones".

From vengeance to justice. In the first two plays, each killing answers the last, and each killer believes justice is on his or her side. The trilogy ends when the cycle passes to a public court: evidence, argument, a vote, and an outcome both sides must accept.

Athenians watching in 458 BC knew the real Areopagus council, whose powers had just been cut back in reforms of 462/1 BC. Scholars still debate whether the play supports, regrets or simply accepts those reforms.
Thinking the Furies are simply defeated. They are not driven out; they are given an honored place. The play suggests that a city still needs some respect and fear of wrongdoing, under the law.

deep.html: Three poets were chosen each year for the City Dionysia. Each presented three tragedies and a satyr play on one day. The actors were all men, wore masks, and could play several parts each. The chorus, twelve in Aeschylus' day, sang and danced between the scenes. Violent acts happened offstage and were reported or revealed afterward.

items: Clytemnestra, Orestes and the Furies all claim to be doing justice. Can more than one side be right?
Why does Athena found a court instead of deciding the case herself?
Is "wisdom comes by suffering" a comfort or a warning?
What is the difference between revenge and punishment?

deep.html: Sophocles and Euripides both wrote their own Electra, each telling the same revenge differently, which you can compare on the next rungs. Aristotle's Poetics studies how tragedies like these work. In the Middle Ages and after, the idea that a court, not a family, should answer a killing became a basic principle of law.

questions: In the trilogy, each act of revenge leads to another. How do people stop a cycle like that, in families or between countries?
Athena asks ordinary citizens to be the jury. Why might that be better than letting a god or a king decide?
The jury's vote is a tie. Is it fair that Athena's vote decides?
The Furies are offered honor instead of being punished. Why might that work better?
The watchman waits a whole year for a signal fire. What is the longest you have waited for news?
care: The plays turn on killings within a family. They take place offstage and are told, not shown; this lesson summarizes them without detail. Young readers can focus on Athena's trial and the Furies' change of heart.
